entries.title: add parent/child regions
entries.body:
`nish:region` gains `child(f)` and `childWith(arg, f)`. Each makes a region whose parent is the region entered now. A child may point into its parent's memory without copying it, because the parent outlives every child: `free(parent)` frees its children, deepest first, and retires their handles, so a later use of a copied child handle panics as stale. `free(child)` unlinks one child. A plain `region()` made inside `enter` stays independent, so existing programs keep their meaning.

What a child may keep is the parent memory that existed before the current `enter`: what the root `enter` handed in reaches. Memory the `enter`'s `f` allocated may be released by a pass scope while the child lives, so storing it into a child is NL2610. That includes fresh memory stored into the root and read back, and a write through a root node aliased in a fresh object. Child memory stored into the parent or into outer memory is NL2609. Growing parent memory from a child is NL2615. A parent object as the child's root is NL2614. A child's builder may keep parent nodes in lists and maps it allocates. `child`/`childWith` outside an `enter` or `enterWith` function, directly or through a callee, is the new NL2702. In a parallel body or a spawned function it is NL2351, as `region` is. A plain `Region<T>` that reaches `enter` through a parameter, field or element is judged as a possible child when the program makes a `child<T>`. LANGUAGE.md states these limits.

Runtime: each region slot gains a parent handle and an intrusive child list, linked through slot indices (96 bytes a slot, was 80). Child create, free and unlink are O(1) per child, and the cascading free is iterative. Freeing a tree with any member entered panics before anything is freed. `awaitAll` lanes never adopt a child or a parent with children (recorded in docs/security/async.md). `runtime/nish.mjs` mirrors all of this under Node.

`src/` cannot use `child` or `childWith` until a release ships them (the rolling freeze).

entries.title: explain which loops and functions keep their memory (--explain-memory)
entries.body:
* feat(cli): explain which loops and functions keep their memory (--explain-memory)

`nish compile --explain-memory` (and `nish run --explain-memory`) prints, on
stderr after the warnings, every loop and function of the program's own
modules that keeps what it allocates past its scope, and why: the line that
stores the allocation, the outer variable that holds it, the array older than
the pass that grows, or the callee that stores it. Each line also says where
the memory does go back - the end of an enclosing scoped pass or
`using a = arena()` block, the function's return, the caller's release, or,
in `main`, never. A loop condition or `for` update that allocates on every
pass is listed on its own line. A summary counts the allocating loops and
scalar-result functions and how many of each keep their memory, so a CI job
can hold the report against a golden.

The warnings name a refused scope only where they can name a rewrite; the
report names every one, so a lost pass scope shows up at compile time rather
than as a memory ceiling in production. The IR is unchanged; `--emit-ast`,
`--json` and `--fix` refuse the flag (exit 2).

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#explaining-kept-memory
Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory

* fix(cli): explain-memory names every allocating loop and head

Review fixes to --explain-memory. A loop whose pass calls a function that
answers a number but leaves memory behind now counts as allocating, read
from the call graph rather than the sites that return memory. A loop the
scope decision never reached is still explained, a body that declares
`using a = arena()` after statements that allocate nothing is the program's
own bracket, a condition and an update that both allocate each get a line,
and a do...while condition follows the loops of its body. Under
--no-elision every allocating loop is listed. The report now prints ahead of
the --capabilities line, which stays last on stderr.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory

* fix(cli): explain-memory follows constructors, callback functions and brackets

Review fixes to --explain-memory. A `new` whose constructor leaves memory
counts as an allocating call, as the pass walk charges it. A function that
takes a function parameter, or is generic, is explained through its first
instantiation instead of not at all. A function is listed only when an
allocation is still held at its return, so one bracketed by its own
`using a = arena()` or allocating only inside scoped passes is counted and
not listed, and its line names the line of what it keeps. The pass decision
no longer scans a pass it refuses for `Arena.mark`; only the report does.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* fix(cli): explain-memory names a leaking callee and every instantiation

A function that keeps memory only because a callee lets an allocation
outlive its call now names that callee, instead of blaming a local of its
own. Every instantiation of a generic or callback-taking function is
explained under its own name, not only the first, and a loop that calls a
function the analysis cannot see is counted as allocating. The --help line
fits in 80 columns, and the released-range scan proves its index in range,
so src/ gains no performance warning.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* fix(cli): explain-memory names the function a leak starts in

A function that keeps memory because a callee lets an allocation outlive
the call now names the function down its calls whose own leak it is,
rather than the first callee on the path. A kept allocation made by a
call or a `new` names that callee, and one the analysis cannot see into
says so; a function that keeps an array literal of its own, with no
callee to blame, says that instead of a generic line.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* fix(cli): explain-memory blames the right function and lists unseen callees

A function that reads `Arena.mark` is no longer told that is why it keeps
memory: the mark refuses a pass its scope, not the function's. A `new` of
the function's own whose constructor allocates nothing is the allocation
kept, not a call to blame. The search for where a leak starts passes over
recursion, and the line says the doubt passes up every call rather than that
the callee lets memory outlive it, since that callee's own scope may give it
back. A loop with no scope that calls a function the analysis cannot see is
listed even when another refusal came first.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* fix(cli): explain-memory names a function's own leak first

A function that holds an allocation of its own where the analysis cannot
prove it dead is told so, even when it also calls a function that leaks: the
callee's fix would not give it its scope back. The facts record that own leak
apart from the one that flows up from callees. A pass whose every allocation
goes back with a `using a = arena()` block or a scoped loop nested inside it
keeps nothing and is no longer listed, and a constructor, which answers the
object it builds, is not listed as a function.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* fix(cli): explain-memory stops at a callee's own leak and reports under --deny-retention

A function that keeps memory names its own leak first, ahead of any callee,
and the leak-root walk stops at the first callee whose leak is its own
rather than following it further down. The own-leak reason now covers every
way an allocation is held (a local assigned more than once, an array of its
own, or a callee that keeps its argument). A build --deny-retention refuses
still prints the report after its errors, since it says why each refused
loop keeps its memory.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* fix(cli): explain-memory names the line a function's own leak is on

A function that holds an allocation of its own now names the line of that
allocation, read from the sites the escape analysis marked as leaking,
rather than the first kept node, which could be an unrelated call above it.
NISH_CHECK_PROPAGATE compares the new own-leak fact between the worklist and
whole passes, and the language reference says which refused builds still
print the report.

Tests: tests/cases/explain_memory_calls

* refactor(cli): explain-memory reads --no-elision from the facts

The report reads whether elision is off from the facts table it explains
instead of a parameter threaded through five functions, picks a loop's
condition with a switch on the node kind, and names no line for a
function's own leak when the analysis recorded no site for it rather than
an unrelated one.

* fix(cli): keep Compilation free of padding after factsSettled

The factsSettled flag sits beside the other booleans, so Compilation stays
208 bytes and the performance ratchet's NL9010 baseline holds.

entries.title: serve answers pipelined requests in one write
entries.body:
serve used to answer a burst of pipelined requests one request per loop turn, with one write for each answer. Under wrk's 16-deep plaintext pipeline, every connection paid for 16 turns and 16 system calls.

serve now opts its HttpHandler into deferred sends with `deferSends()`:
- While a connection's output still has room, it is not draining, its write is not held, and no request on it is parked, the handler puts the send off and records the connection as owed.
- `flush()`, which serve calls once per turn and `wait()` calls before it polls, then writes each owed connection once.
- serve takes every queued request on a connection before it parks. An answering task no longer writes the wake byte while the loop is awake.

A handler that never calls `deferSends()` sends each answer as soon as it ends, exactly as before. That covers the explicit HttpHandler loop, upstream and the Postgres carrier, and `wait()` keeps its timeout for them. One change reaches every handler: a write the socket could not take whole stays armed for writing after a flush empties the output. Before, the rest of such a response could stall.

`ServeStats.sends` and `HttpHandler.sends()` count the sends.

The security records are HANDLER-13 and SERVE-16; both hold. A parked request that a flush lets in is recorded as not pinned by a test.
metrics: wrk with the server on CPU 0 and medians of 3 rounds of 10 s. On plaintext pipelined 16 deep, async rose to 7.7x/5.9x/5.4x/2.7x its base at c=256/1024/4096/16384, against an entry vs entry-copy band of 3.7/3.0/4.4/7.7%. On json, async against the explicit entry moved from -8.6/-13.9/-1.0/-8.4/-13.2/-22.2% to -20.5/-0.8/-8.3/-5.7/-23.3/-13.6% at c=16/32/64/128/256/512. That is mixed, with bands up to 13.9%, and is recorded open. The explicit entry is unchanged.

entries.title: refuse the mistakes every type accepts
entries.body:
Six new errors for lines that type-check and still cannot be what their
author meant, the bugs rustc warns about and Clippy denies, made errors here
because each is a bug far more often than a choice and a model writing the
program acts on an error where it may skim a warning:

- NL2712: a local nothing reads, or only stores into (`n++` that nothing
  reports). A `for...of` binding counts; a name starting with `_` is exempt.
- NL2713: a statement with no call, store or `await` in it (`a === b;`).
- NL2714: a value assigned to itself (`p.x = p.x`).
- NL2715: the same pure operand on both sides of a comparison, `&&`, `||`,
  a bitwise operator, `-`, `/` or `%`. On a float only `<` and `>` are
  refused, so `x !== x` stays the NaN test.
- NL2716: an `else if` that repeats an earlier condition of its chain.
- NL2717: an unsigned value compared with 0 for its sign (`u < 0`).

The findings come from `src/hygiene.ts`, a walk over each body that checked
cleanly, and are held until every other rule has passed, so a program with
any other error is told that error alone. The program's own package and the
standard library are held to them; a dependency's are left to its author.
They found an unused local in the Huffman length limiter of
`std/compress/deflate.ts`, which is deleted.

The language reference's wide tables are re-laid out: each is a summary
table of short cells followed by one entry per row, saying what the call
does for someone writing Nish, with how it compiles and the tests that pin
it beneath. The checker's refusals and the panic sites become lists, and the
Types section reads from which type to write, through what differs from
TypeScript, to how each type sits in memory and crosses to C.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#mistakes-every-type-accepts
Tests: tests/cases/reject_unread_local, reject_no_effect_statement,
reject_self_assign, reject_same_operands, reject_repeated_condition,
reject_unsigned_zero, reject_hygiene_held, hygiene_quiet;

entries.title: the async Postgres pool pipelines queries across tasks
entries.body:
PgAsyncPool can now share a connection among many tasks.

`pgAsyncSeat` takes a seat on the least-seated connection, waiting in a FIFO queue when every connection is at its depth (8 by default). Each seated task sends its statement with its own Sync. That statement is prepared once per connection under a name and re-prepared after a re-dial, so many statements from different tasks are in flight on one connection at once. `pgAsyncTurn` waits for the task's answer to come round, in send order, and `pgAsyncDone` gives the seat back.

A waiting claim or seat is woken when a connection or seat is released, through a socket pair opened on first wait, instead of sleep-polling 1–16 ms. A task cancelled while queued leaves the queue. A task cancelled with its answer unread has that answer read past, so the statements behind it are not disturbed. If that answer cannot be read past (too large, a ParameterStatus, a transaction left open), the statements behind it fail and the connection closes, as before (PG-43). The startup is bounded by `connectWaitMs`.

The async TechEmpower database entry moves onto the seated pool. It re-dials a closed slot with a bounded backoff.

The security record adds PG-39 to PG-44 to docs/security/postgres.md:
- the wake accounting, whose two fixes (a woken waiter spinning on an unread wake byte, and a wake lost while one was pending) are each pinned by a test section that fails without it;
- the password held for re-dials;
- the wake pairs' descriptor cost, up to `size` + 129 socket pairs.
metrics: the async /db entry, median of 3 rounds of wrk on one machine, rises from about 11k to about 30k req/s at c=64. The explicit entry is at about 108k, so async stays about 3.5–4x behind it at c≥64. /fortunes at c≥64 is slower than the previous async pool (22219 vs 25985 at c=64, 16481 vs 23373 at c=256), with the cause unmeasured and recorded open. The explicit entry is unchanged.

entries.title: add spawnPipedWithin, a captured run with a deadline
entries.body:
`spawnPipedWithin(argv, stdin, stdout, stderr, timeoutMs)` runs a child with
its stdout and stderr captured, as `spawnPiped` does, and kills it with SIGKILL
once `timeoutMs` milliseconds have passed. It then answers -3, and the bytes
read before the kill stay in the arrays. A negative `timeoutMs` means no
deadline, so `spawnPiped(...)` is `spawnPipedWithin(..., -1)`. The other
answers are `spawnPiped`'s: the exit code, 128 + the signal, -1, and -2 for a
stream over 16 MiB.

The deadline is read from the monotonic clock and also bounds the final wait.
A child that closes both streams and then hangs still ends at the deadline.
Only the child's pid is killed: a grandchild that holds a pipe open keeps
running, and can turn the child's exit into -3.

The builtin is exported from `nish:process` and needs the `process.spawn`
capability. wasm32 refuses it (NL2404), the WASI build answers -1, and the Node
host passes the deadline to `spawnSync` as its `timeout`. `spawnPiped`'s IR
does not move.

entries.title: add toFixed and split with a limit to nish/text
entries.body:
nish/text gains the last two pieces of WP34's N10.

toFixed(x, n) is JavaScript's Number.prototype.toFixed. The answer is
the decimal with n fraction digits closest to the exact binary value of
x, and a tie takes the larger one. That gives (1.005).toFixed(2) as
"1.00" and (2.5).toFixed(0) as "3". |x| >= 1e21 answers String(x), NaN
answers "NaN", -0 drops its sign, and a negative value that rounds to
zero keeps it. n outside 0..100 panics, where JavaScript throws a
RangeError. It is written in Nish with exact multi-digit arithmetic, so
the native and Node readings run the same code and agree.

splitLimit(text, sep, limit) is text.split(sep, limit). It keeps the
first `limit` pieces and drops the rest. A limit of 0 gives [], and a
negative limit keeps every piece, as Node's ToUint32 reading does. An
empty separator panics, as it does for split. split itself is unchanged.

Both are tested against Node: every expected line is checked with
JavaScript's own answer. Their refusals are pinned too. The guide, the
language reference and the library reference cover them.

entries.title: read a file a window at a time with fileOpen, fileReadAt, fileSize and fileClose
entries.body:
Four builtins, global and exported by `nish:fs`, read a regular file through a buffer the program owns. Memory follows the window rather than the file, and a file past 2^31 − 1 bytes is readable.

`fileOpen(path)` answers a plain `i32` descriptor or a negated Linux errno. It opens with `O_RDONLY | O_CLOEXEC | O_NONBLOCK`, and anything that is not a regular file is refused: a directory is -21, anything else -22. `fileReadAt(fd, buf, off, len, pos)` is a positional `pread` into `buf[off, off + len)`. The window is bounds-checked as `netRead`'s is. A negative `pos`, or a `pos + len` past 2^63 − 1, answers -22. A negative or closed descriptor answers -9. `fileSize` answers an `i64`, and `fileClose` is never retried. Errors map by errno name to Linux's numbers on every platform; any code outside the documented set is -5.

All four are `fs.read`, refused in `scope()` tasks and under `--deny fs.read`. Under Node they answer byte for byte as natively. `--profile wasi` links them through `runtime-os.c`. A freestanding `wasm32` build is refused at check time (NL2718). `runtime-wasm.c` defines them answering -38, so a `--profile wasm` link never fails; this adds 105 bytes to every such module.

Records the maintainer's answers to WP44's Q1–Q9 (every recommendation accepted), ticks F1 and F2, and adds security record RT-50.

entries.title: typed JSON decodes and encodes tagged unions
entries.body:
nish/json-typed now reads and writes a tagged union of classes wherever a class may appear: as the top-level value, a field, a `| null` field, an array element, and a Map value. A program no longer needs a hand-written decoder over json-value for each union, so the schema and the decoder cannot drift apart.

- **The tag.** On the wire, a variant's tag is the name of its enum member, unless the variant gives `static readonly json = { tag: "..." }`. The tag's key is the union's tag field, which the existing `rename` option can rename.
- **Encoding** writes the tag first, as that string.
- **Decoding** finds the tag wherever it sits in the object. When the tag is the first key it takes a fast path; otherwise it reads ahead and rewinds. The read-ahead costs at most maxDepth + 1 passes over the input, recorded as JSON-17 in docs/security/json.md.
- **Bad tags.** A missing tag, a tag that is not a string, or an unknown tag answers the new JSON_DECODE_TAG (-26).
- **New call.** jsonDecodeUnion(d, prev) decodes a top-level union. It reuses prev when the tag matches prev's variant, and otherwise makes a new variant. jsonEncode accepts a union unchanged. No existing call shape changes.
- **Generated code.** Each union gets one decode function and one encode function, so a recursive union such as Expr = Num | Neg | Add compiles to plain recursive calls.
- **Language change.** A union, or an array or nullable of one, may now be a Map's value type argument. A union is still refused everywhere else as a type argument (NL2533).
- **New refusals.** Six codes cover: a variant that is not a class; a class with a `tag` but no enum-member field; two variants with the same wire tag; variants that disagree on the tag key; a `tag` that is not a string literal; and jsonDecode called on a union. They also fire when a union is reached only through a Map value.

entries.title: a held HTTP/1 write keeps the write bit once a flush empties the output
entries.body:
Http1Server armed a connection with no interest when a held write met an emptied output. The sequence: a short write set writeHeld, next answered H1_NEED_MORE on EAGAIN, the peer drained the socket, and flush emptied the output. wantsWrite() was then false, and inputRoom() was 0. The slot was re-armed with events=0, so the response never finished. This was the intermittent "file-server: the 64 MiB file arrives whole to a stalling reader" timeout on main.

entries.title: refuse a granted program's interpreter as a spawn target under --sandbox (SBX-1)
entries.body:
Under --sandbox, a dependency granted process.spawn=<program> can now start only that program. The exec allowlist must grant EXECUTE on each granted program's ELF loader and #! interpreter, because the kernel opens them to start it; until now a dependency could also spawn that loader directly and have it run any binary on the machine (SBX-1, High). The compiler now marks an interpreter the grant does not name itself with a second leading slash in @.sandbox.exec (the same file to the kernel, so the Landlock rules and nish_sandbox's signature are unchanged). The runtime records each marked file's identity before confinement and refuses a spawn whose target is one of them with EACCES. The target is resolved as posix_spawnp would resolve it and executed through the descriptor that was checked (/proc/self/fd/N), so a symlink, a hardlink or a name swapped between the check and the exec cannot reach the loader. A program the grant names explicitly stays spawnable even when it is also another's interpreter.

Spawning under --sandbox with a marked entry now needs /proc mounted, best-effort mode included; a #! script sees /proc/self/fd/N as $0. SBX-1 is recorded fixed in docs/security/sandbox.md, and CodeQL's new cpp/path-injection alert on the PATH lookup is triaged as not a defect in docs/security/runtime.md. WP37 moves to 4 of 8; its remaining stages are deferred.

With only that fix reverted, 1 of 10 runs under load stalled, with the server in epoll_wait and both sockets' queues empty; with it restored, 10 of 10 pass. entries.title: copy QUIC stream bytes by slice, not by byte
entries.body:
QuicStreams.write, read and onStream now move bytes between the caller's array and the ring with copyBytes, which is one memmove natively. Each copy is at most two runs: to the ring's end, then from its start. quicPacketCopy clips its run to both windows once and copies it with one copyBytes.

The acknowledgement and receive bitmaps stay one bit per byte, but every walk over them now works a range at a time. The ragged ends of a run are set bit by bit, the whole bytes between them with one fill, and a scan for the end of a set run passes over a full byte at once. The per-byte 64-bit modulo is gone: QuicStream.at runs once per run, and the wrap compares against the ring size. Nothing on the wire changes, and every net_quic* and net_http3* link test passes with its expected output unchanged.

A new tests/link/net_quic_stream case drives a 1,001-byte ring, whose last bitmap byte is partial, through unaligned straddling writes, reads and ACK ranges. It checks byte-exact delivery and checks recvContiguous and sendBase against a bit-per-byte model.

Measured: callgrind Ir per 8 kB h3-load request (net_interop_server, 60 minus 10 requests, over 50): 2,440,035 before (main), 1,450,770 after, -40.5 %. A repeat of the base run gave 2,440,138, a noise band of about ±0.01 %.

entries.title: design note for QUIC on more than one core
entries.body:
docs/h3-multicore.md designs how prefork workers sharing one UDP port keep each QUIC connection on the process that owns it, so a peer that changes address is not hashed to another worker and reset.

Every server-issued connection ID carries the owning worker's index in byte 0. A classic BPF program attached with SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_CBPF steers each datagram by that byte, modulo the worker count N, so a packet's worker depends on its DCID alone and never on the client's address. The supervisor binds the UDP group first and carries N to the runtime in udpBind's flag bits 8-15 and to each worker in --nish-prefork-udp=<fd>,<N>. Workers take their index and N through QuicServerConfig, range-checked 0 <= k < N <= 255. UDP GRO is refused on a steered socket, because one coalesced flow can hold several connections. A refused attach falls back to one worker before any TCP listener is bound.

Measured: cBPF steering 64/64 to the named socket, out-of-range indices fall back to the 4-tuple hash, unprivileged attach works; eBPF needs CAP_BPF (estimates are labelled as such in the note).

entries.title: expose x509 criticality, AKI issuer/serial and AIA to pki
entries.body:
X509Certificate now records three things it previously parsed and dropped: the critical flag of each extension it decodes, whether the authorityKeyIdentifier carries authorityCertIssuer or a serial, and whether authorityInfoAccess is well formed. A certificate whose authorityInfoAccess is malformed no longer parses.

nish/crypto/pki uses these to refuse the markings RFC 5280 forbids:
- a non-critical basicConstraints on an issuer
- a critical authorityKeyIdentifier anywhere on the path
- a policyConstraints that is not critical
- a root whose authorityKeyIdentifier lacks a key identifier or names an issuer and serial
- a leaf whose subjectAltName criticality does not match an empty subject
- a leaf with a critical extKeyUsage

Trust anchors are held to the same marking rules; every root in Debian's Mozilla-derived bundle conforms. Nine limbo divergences close (30 → 21); the public-suffix item stays open (PKI-28).

entries.title: ship the SSSE3 and NEON Adler-32 kernels
entries.body:
adler32Update now runs a vector kernel in the runtime: SSSE3 on x86-64 and NEON on little-endian AArch64.
- The kernel is chosen once per process. x86-64 reads cpuid leaf 1 for SSSE3; NEON is AArch64's baseline.
- NISH_ADLER32=soft (exact match) pins the Nish loop.
- Every other target, and wasm, keeps the Nish loop.

It uses the seam CRC-32 uses. adlerUpdate checks its window, then branches on nish_adler32_hw() between nish_adler32_update in runtime/runtime-checksum.c and the private adler32Walk, which is the former loop. The two arms join at a phi, so the answer at the edges is still the std file's. The kernels work in 32-byte blocks and reduce mod 65521 after at most 173 blocks (5,536 bytes), inside the 32-bit bound from an unreduced seed.

entries.title: QUIC sends datagrams past 1,200 bytes after path MTU discovery
entries.body:
QUIC connections now run DPLPMTUD (RFC 9000 §14.3, RFC 8899). Once the handshake is confirmed and the path validated, a connection with nothing else to send probes a larger datagram (PADDING and PING) up to the smaller of the peer's max_udp_payload_size, 1,452 bytes and a carrier's pathMtuLimit. An acknowledged probe raises the path MTU; a lost one costs no congestion response and never counts toward persistent congestion. Three loss events of full-size packets fall back to 1,200 and restart the search, and a new path starts again from 1,200. The congestion window, minimum window and pacer follow the datagram size (RFC 9002).

The relay's DATA-down limit of 1,164 bytes is gone on a path that has validated more.

Known limit: a sender that always has data queued probes only between flights (recorded in docs/security/quic.md).

Refs: docs/security/quic.md

entries.title: the review tier of fix in --json
entries.body:
A portability warning whose site has a rewrite that makes both readings
agree now carries it under a new `--json` key, `review`: a sibling of
`fix` with the same edit-list shape, printed after it and only when there
are edits. `fix` keeps its meaning (every edit in it is safe to apply
blind), every existing `--json` line is unchanged, and `nish --fix` never
applies a review edit. An agent applies one from `--json` and checks the
site, as docs/AI.md describes.

NL8006 (integer `/`) is the first row with one: the quotient wrapped in its
type's own conversion, `toI32(a / b)` (or `toU8`, `toU16`, `toU32`), and
`q /= d` rewritten to `q = toI32(q / d)`. Applied, the program compiles to
byte-identical IR with the warning gone and prints the same under Node.
There is no edit in a generic body, for `/=` on anything but a plain name,
on a ranged target, with a divisor that holds a `/` or a comment before the
operator, for `i64`/`u64`, where operand types differ, or where the module
binds the conversion's name. NL8007 and NL8008 get none: no rewrite reads
the same under Node without warning again or costing an instruction.

The range proof now carries a quotient's range through a conversion to its
own type, so a hand-written `toI32(a / 4) + 1` skips the overflow check
`a / 4 + 1` already skipped. No nish-cmp corpus program moves.

entries.title: record_size_limit on the TLS server
entries.body:
The TLS 1.3 server reads a client's record_size_limit (RFC 8449) and never sends a protected record whose plaintext passes it: the limit less one for the content type, never above 2^14, applied to every record sealed after EncryptedExtensions (the rest of the flight, NewSessionTicket, application data, KeyUpdate and alerts). When the client offers the extension the server answers with its own limit in EncryptedExtensions. A value under 64 is refused with illegal_parameter, a malformed body with decode_error, a duplicate as any duplicate extension is; a value above 16385 is clamped. The limit is off under QUIC, where records do not apply.

At a client's limit of 64 each record carries 63 bytes of content for 22 bytes of header and tag; at 2^14 the overhead is 0.13%.

Tests: tests/link/net_tls_record_size_limit (and its f64 twin) read the record lengths off the wire at limits of 64 and 512, with and without padding, for the flight and a write; the fullest record is exactly the limit. An openssl s_client -record_size_limit interop runs where OpenSSL has the option and skips with that reason otherwise.
Refs: docs/security/tls.md
Part of #1433

entries.title: declare class as a C struct layout, passed by pointer
entries.body:
A `declare class` now describes a C struct: its fields are laid out in
declaration order at C's natural alignment, never reordered, with pointer
fields sized for the target, so the compiler computes the same offsets and
size clang does. `new Name()` zero-fills every byte, padding included. A
`declare function` parameter typed as a layout class takes a pointer to it,
borrowed for the call: C may read and write it while the call runs and must
not keep it.

A layout field is u8, u16, u32, u64, i32, i64, f32, f64, CPtr, CPtr | null
or another layout nested by value. `number` is refused by any spelling,
since its width would follow --number-mode. A layout never crosses by value,
never sits in an array, and never appears, directly or held by another type,
in an exported signature, so no header, .d.ts or N-API binding describes one;
a build whose target is not fixed (--emit-dts, a page module) refuses it.
The design is docs/wp27-ffi.md §9; S4.2, copying a C-owned struct out of a
CPtr, follows.

entries.title: parse an HTTP/1 request head a vector at a time
entries.body:
The request parser in nish/net/http1-codec now finds line ends, CR/LF and control bytes sixteen bytes at a time across a whole header section, copies the section into the head as the scan loads it, and does its per-line work (OWS trims, the colon check, the framing counts) once per line rather than once per byte. The old parser is frozen in tests/link/net_http1_parse_diff/old.ts and the new one agrees with it on every input fed: the fuzz corpus and regressions, grammar-made requests, every byte at every position, tight limits with the deciding byte at each vector lane, long Cookie and Authorization values with stop bytes at every lane, and a 936-byte browser head split at every point (464,424 cases). docs/security/http1-codec.md records the scan, the mutations the differential catches and the head's layout. entries.title: function references as arguments, `| null` and `Map` values
entries.body:
A function reference can now be passed to a function-typed parameter, be `| null`, and be a `Map` value. Each call through one still compiles to a `switch` dispatcher over the functions that can reach that place, followed by a direct call; no indirect call is emitted.

- Arguments: a local or parameter holding a reference may be passed to an inline function-typed parameter. The call is instantiated once per call site, through an arrow that calls the reference.
  - A field or element argument is refused with "read it into a `const` first" (NL2741).
  - So is a local that a later argument assigns (NL2743), because JavaScript reads the argument before the call and this lowering would read it after.
  - The runners that check the body they are handed (`expose`, `exposeWith`, `parallelMap`, `parallelMapInto`, `parallelReduce`, `spawn`, `region`, `enterWith`) refuse a reference (NL2734).
- `S | null` for a function type S is the one scalar `| null`:
  - Tag 0 is `null`, and `new Array<S | null>(n)` reads `null` in every slot.
  - A call needs a narrowing test first (NL2740, NL2742).
  - A nullable reference is aligned to its 4-byte tag, and `-g` names tag 0 `null`.
- `Map` values may be a reference, an array of references, or a nullable of either. NL2738 is retired.
  - A call through `get` dispatches over the functions stored into the map.
  - A function-typed `Map` key stays refused.
- Each new place joins the per-place pass, including `push`, `for…of` over arrays and `Map` values, `??`, `?:` and assignment expressions.
- The escape-join refusal (NL2736) covers every new place. `fnref_place_set` has argument, nullable and `Map` variants, each keeping `P` on the stack with flat peak RSS at 1x and 10x.
- A reference inside a `Result` arm is refused (NL2744).
- Stage 1 follow-ups (#1417):
  - `<`, `>` and arithmetic on a reference are pinned on their generic codes.
  - The defaulted-parameter refusal is pinned.
  - `JSON.stringify` of a reference gives the function-reference wording.
  - The `nish:` builtin note no longer says no function is a value.
  - The guide documents gdb's two-step into a reference call and `skip -rfu '^\$ref\.'`.

entries.title: cleartext HTTP/2 with prior knowledge
entries.body:
nish/net/http2-cleartext serves HTTP/2 over plain TCP to a client that starts with the connection preface (h2c with prior knowledge; no Upgrade: h2c, which RFC 9113 dropped), on the existing sans-IO http2.ts core, which it does not modify. It reads the 24-byte preface itself, across as many reads as it takes, and closes a connection whose preface is wrong at the first mismatching byte without writing anything. No frame buffer is borrowed before the preface is whole, slots are fixed at construction, and a warmed request allocates nothing. expire() closes a slot whose preface is still incomplete past prefaceTimeout and spares one whose preface has arrived.

It is the cleartext carrier the one-handler façade (docs/http-one-handler.md) builds on, and what h2load and a proxy's upstream speak. Cleartext means no confidentiality; docs/security/http2-cleartext.md records the scope.

Tests: tests/link/net_http2_cleartext covers the exchange, prefaces split at bytes 1, 10 and 23, every refusal, slot exhaustion, expire on incomplete and complete prefaces, a flat Arena over warmed requests, and curl and h2load where they speak HTTP/2; net_http2_cleartext_bad_slots and _bad_timeout pin the panics.

entries.title: Postgres over TLS in the carrier
entries.body:
PgConfig gains tls (PG_TLS_DISABLE, the default; PG_TLS_REQUIRE; PG_TLS_VERIFY_FULL), tlsRootsPath and tlsServerName. With TLS asked for, the carrier sends an SSLRequest, reads exactly one answer byte once all eight request bytes are out, and on S runs nish/net/tls/client on the program's loop without blocking: TLS 1.3 only, verify-full checking the chain against the roots and the host name, require encrypting without verifying. Any answer but S fails the query with PG_ERR_TLS before the StartupMessage leaves; bytes a peer sends after its S go to the record layer and fail the handshake, so nothing reaches the backend parser in the clear. Every path that is not the carrier — PgConnection built directly, pgAsyncConnect, a hand-driven PgPool — panics on a non-zero tls rather than connecting in cleartext. PG-9 is fixed for the carrier; the other paths refuse.

entries.title: a lingering close for HTTP/1.1, SETTINGS and idle timeouts for HTTP/2, a session clock for WebTransport
entries.body:
Three open server findings are fixed, each with a before/after test (WP39 G2).

H1-2: after a refusal on a connection whose client is still sending,
Http1Server shuts its write side and drains what arrives, so the client reads
the 413 or 400 rather than a reset (RFC 9112 9.6). The drain ends at the
client's hang-up, at Http1Config.lingerBytes (default 65,536; 0 closes at once
as before) or at lingerTimeout (default 2 s).

H2-3: Http2Config.settingsTimeout (default 10 s) and idleTimeout (default
60 s). Http2TlsServer.expire sends GOAWAY SETTINGS_TIMEOUT to a peer that has
not acknowledged SETTINGS in time (RFC 9113 6.5.3) and GOAWAY NO_ERROR to one
quiet past the idle timeout, then closes the slot.

WT-2: WebTransportConfig.idleTimeout (default 60 s) and maxDatagramsPerSecond
(default 1,024). expire ends sessions quiet past the timeout and reports them
as WT_CLOSED; datagrams past the rate are dropped and counted in
datagramsDropped.

Every limit is configurable and checked at start-up. H3-5 stays open.

The interop test server's QUIC streams take a 256 KiB window. A stream's send
buffer is sized by maxStreamData, so at 64 KiB one lost packet stopped new
data, and a NAT rebinding in that round trip left the interop runner's
download truncated. A loopback case replays it. The library limit itself is
unchanged and is recorded in #1485.

The three nish-cmp declarations for cleartext HTTP/2 now spell their release
note as the changelog does, which turns nish-cmp green on main again.

entries.title: WP28 spike S2 — async by contagion, counted on real TypeScript

entries.title: WP28 spike S6 — try/catch by landing pads against a Result desugaring
entries.body:
The two candidate lowerings of `try`/`catch` measured on the same three shapes: a hot loop that never throws, a parser that fails one record in 1000, 100 and 10, and a call chain that unwinds 1, 8 and 32 frames. Each shape is the `Result` program the desugaring would produce and hand-written LLVM IR using `invoke` and `landingpad` on the Itanium unwinder, with a small two-phase personality in bench/wp28-s6/unwind.c. run.mjs assembles every `.ll`, builds both sides at the release profile, runs them interleaved, checks the outputs agree and prints time, noise band and section sizes.

The README recommends the `Result` desugaring for C5, for the maintainer to accept. The recommendation rests on targets: WASI and the freestanding profile have no unwinder, and the wasm backend drops the `catch` without a diagnostic. On time, the two are inside the noise band where nothing throws, and a failure costs about 770 ns plus 135 ns a frame by landing pads against about 2 ns plus 1.2 ns a frame by `Result`. One row goes the other way and is recorded: the inlined parser is faster with landing pads because the three-word `Result` return blocks inlining.

The generated self-goldens for the four new bench programs are added. The roadmap tick and the note's §7 land with the stage that records the spikes.

entries.title: steer QUIC packets to the owning process
entries.body:
Prefork workers can now share one UDP port for QUIC. The kernel hands each datagram to the worker whose index is byte 0 of the destination connection ID, so a connection stays with its worker when the client's address or port changes.

udpBind takes a new flag 4 that attaches a classic-BPF SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_CBPF program reading DCID byte 0 modulo the group count (bits 8-15, 1 to 255). QuicServerConfig gains workerIndex and workerCount; with a valid pair every server-issued connection ID (first SCID, NEW_CONNECTION_ID, Retry SCID) carries the worker index, and a listener drops a sibling worker's short header instead of sending a stateless reset that would end the sibling's connection. PreforkConfig.listenUdp binds one steered socket per worker before the TCP listeners and hands it over with --nish-prefork-udp=<fd>,<N>, read by preforkUdpListener and preforkUdpCount; if the kernel refuses the attach, the supervisor runs one worker on a plain socket and says so on stderr.

Every QuicServerConfig literal now sets workerIndex: -1 and workerCount: 0 (Nish interfaces have no optional fields). The new security record docs/security/quic-multicore.md (QM-1 to QM-5) covers the UDP path; the guide's networking page has a multi-core QUIC section.

entries.title: readStruct copies a C-owned struct out of a CPtr
entries.body:
`readStruct(p)` in `nish:unsafe` copies the struct a `CPtr` points at into a
fresh, Nish-owned `declare class` instance, so the result never aliases C
memory: C may free or overwrite the original and the copy keeps its values.
The layout comes from the context type (`const lc: Lconv = readStruct(p)`),
since a type argument is never written at a call site. A NULL pointer is
tested before the copy and panics with the `ffi-null` kind, so
`--deny-panics` refuses the call; the copy is the caller's allocation, held
by the arena like `new`, and it lowers the same on wasm32, where the layout
is sized for 4-byte pointers. The call needs the `unsafe` capability and has
no Node form. With S4.1 this completes WP27 S4.

entries.title: a bare --compat that accepts nothing, and the erasure invariant that holds it
entries.body:
`--compat` now parses. It is the dialect flag of the compatibility-mode proposal with no feature behind it yet: it admits no construct and changes no lowering, and `--compat=<anything>` is a usage error. `--help`, the CLI guide page and LANGUAGE.md's flag list say so.

What holds it to that is a new test, tests/compat-erasure.js, wired into the suite as the `compat-erasure` section: every positive tests/cases program is compiled with and without the flag and its output compared byte for byte, and every `reject_*` case must reject with the same exit code, diagnostic code and words. A self-test feeds the harness a compiler wrapper that alters one IR line, one diagnostic word and one code under `--compat` and expects each to be caught by name. The harness compares each case under its own `.args` and `.env`; the suite's second compiles with other flags are not yet compared.

This is spike S3 of docs/wp28-compatibility-mode.md §7.1 and the acceptance test the next stage, C0, is held to.

entries.title: WP28 spike S4 — Promise.all as a fork/join against parallelReduce
entries.body:
Whether the second payoff of docs/wp28-compatibility-mode.md §6.4 is real, measured: two non-interfering calls joined on `using s = scope()`, written by hand as `--async-model threads` would lower a two-call `Promise.all`, against the same two calls made in sequence and against `parallelReduce` over the same work. bench/wp28-s4/ holds the three programs over one kernel, a harness that builds them, runs them interleaved with a byte-identical copy of the baseline for the noise band, checks the checksums agree and prints medians and the break-even task size, and a README with the figures and the fork/join site's IR.

The payoff is real above a task of about 16 µs and a loss below it: a fork/join of two tasks costs about 16 µs more than the work it shares out. `parallelReduce` is a single block on the calling thread below 2^20 elements, so it only forks at the largest size, where it uses more than the two cores a two-call `Promise.all` can. The hand-lowering covers one callee over one array argument; different callees would need the arrow-capture form, which is not measured. How a lowering tells cheap calls from expensive ones is left to the design.

The generated self-goldens for the new bench programs are added. The roadmap tick and the note's §7 land with the stage that records the spikes.

entries.title: cErrno, errno zeroed before and saved after a foreign call
entries.body:
`cErrno()` in `nish:unsafe` reads the errno the most recent `declare function`
call left on this thread. In a program that names it anywhere, the compiler
sets errno to 0 immediately before every foreign call and copies it into a
thread-local runtime slot immediately after, before a string result is
copied or anything else runs, so the runtime's own allocation cannot disturb
it and a C function that reports failure only through errno (strtol out of
range) can be checked. The runtime reads errno in C, so each libc keeps its
own definition and the compiler never names `__errno_location` or `__error`;
`declare let errno` stays refused. A program that never names `cErrno` emits
exactly the IR it did before. A freestanding wasm32 build refuses it. With
S4, this completes WP27: Calling C is landed, 5 of 5.

entries.body:

end. It now puts the body and lets end make the one pass, so serve and
every program that answers with send, sendFields or empty takes one fewer
trip through the carrier per answer. A connection that closes in that pass
now answers HANDLER_SENT where the two-pass path answered HANDLER_DROPPED,
as end always has. serveTask still copies its request: the region rules
refuse a task that reads the server's, and docs/security/serve.md records
why and how long each side lives.

entries.title: recycle a finished task's frame and region instead of freeing them
entries.body:
A spawned task that ends now hands its region back with its node. The next
spawn of the same async function on that node makes no region, and when it
fits the chunk the last one left (at most 64 KiB, and 16 MiB across all
free nodes) it asks malloc for nothing, so a request's task on an async
server costs no malloc, free or region teardown. What a wait asks of the
kernel is unchanged. The kept chunk is not zeroed, as arena memory never
is; docs/security/async.md, ASYNC-20, records why nothing can read or point
into it. The runtime-async.c text budget moves from 3,840 to 4,096 bytes
(3,910 measured).

entries.title: hold a granted program's descendants to the exec grant
entries.body:
Under --sandbox, a dependency granted process.spawn=<program> runs that program, but a granted program's descendants could still reach the loader the exec allowlist must carry for it. Each program started under an exec allowlist now gets exactly one exec: the spawn installs a seccomp user-notification filter on its child, lets that child's own exec through, and closes the listener, after which the kernel refuses every later exec in the subtree. A granted program therefore cannot start a second program, granted or not; a granted #! script runs its builtins only. Grant process.spawn whole for a program that must start helpers.

The spawn runs on two helper threads with a private descriptor table and every signal blocked, so no other thread can swap the checked program or reach the runtime's own descriptors, and the child starts with the caller's signal mask. Where the kernel or container cannot install or answer the filter (Linux before 5.0, a launcher's own listener, a profile that denies unshare), the spawn is refused with one line on stderr, in strict and best-effort alike. Builds without --sandbox are unchanged.

entries.title: build a repeated HTTP/1 response head once per Date tick
entries.body:
Http1Connection.respond keeps the last final response head it wrote and copies its bytes when the next head would be identical except for Date: same status, framing, Connection, field count, and every name and value byte for byte, against the same HttpDate and its once-a-second tick. The head is rebuilt when the date reformats, so a kept head never carries a stale Date or another response's fields. Reuse is generic: any status, fields and body length a handler repeats, with no branch on a path, a header set or the TechEmpower entry. A refused value cannot be reported as written, because value lengths are compared as well as bytes, and the reserved-name and field-text checks still run on every written head.

A miss stays cheap. The buffer is made only once a head repeats its shape, after a few misses in a row the connection stops comparing for the rest of that second, and a slot's kept head is cleared when the slot restarts. docs/security/http1-codec.md records the kept head (H1-7). TFB's rules are kept: Server and Date on every response, Date re-rendered once a second, and the body written per request.

entries.title: prove vector loads and stores in range and tag them as element data
entries.body:
The bounds pass now proves a nish:simd load or store in range when its index and every lane it reaches are covered by facts the pass already holds: a guard such as `i <= n - 16` against a length bound, a hoisted `n` known to be at most the length, or a literal index on an array of known minimum length. The emitter then drops the runtime check for that access. The same reach facts also prove scalar `xs[i + k]` accesses. A proof is withdrawn wherever the length or the index can change: a call that may shrink the array, a pop or length write, a store to the field holding the array, a reassignment of the index. A literal or offset whose last lane would pass INT_MAX keeps its check. Proven vector accesses also carry the element type's TBAA tag and alias scopes, as a scalar element access does, so LLVM can keep a field load across a vector store.

Eight negative cases pin that an out-of-range access still panics: an index not known non-negative, a pop inside the loop, a pop through a second handle, a field array swapped by a callee, the strict and below guard forms, and huge literal and offset indices.
